meta.description: No, Gandhi didn't say it. The closest documented antecedent is Arleen Lorrance's 1974 line "be the change you want to see happen"; Gandhi's real 1913 words were longer and different.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be the change you wish to see in the world'?
meta.ogDescription: The internet's favorite Gandhi quote isn't his. The closest documented match is Arleen Lorrance's 1974 line "be the change you want to see happen" — while Gandhi's genuine 1913 thought was longer.

answer.label: Not Mahatma Gandhi — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1869–1948 · leader of the Indian independence movement
answer.sourceLine: Gandhi almost certainly never spoke or wrote these exact words: no address, letter, or article in his vast published record contains them, and the earliest close match — “be the change you want to see happen” — traces to American educator Arleen Lorrance in 1974. What Gandhi did write, in Indian Opinion in 1913, was the related but far longer thought that “if we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change.”

source.excerpt: We but mirror the world. All the tendencies present in the outer world are to be found in the world of our body. If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change. As a man changes his own nature, so does the attitude of the world change towards him. … We need not wait to see what others do.
trail: Quote Investigator (2017) finds no solid citation tying the phrase to Gandhi and identifies Arleen Lorrance’s 1974 “be the change you want to see happen” as the earliest close match.
Wikiquote reproduces Gandhi’s genuine 1913 “We but mirror the world” passage and notes he did not say the popular six-word version.
The authentic passage is documented in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. XII, from Indian Opinion, 9 August 1913.
source.excerptNote: Gandhi’s actual 1913 words — the closest thing in his writings to the modern slogan, and visibly not the same sentence.
source.rightsNote: The popular six-word wording has no single documented author, so no clean copyright status can be asserted for it. Its closest identifiable coinage — Arleen Lorrance’s 1974 phrasing — is a modern, post-1930 work and therefore certainly not public domain. Gandhi’s genuine 1913 passage, by contrast, is old enough to be public domain, but it is a different text and not the quote in question.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: Who was Mahatma Gandhi?
author.metaLine: 1869–1948 · Leader of Indian independence & apostle of nonviolence
author.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi led India’s independence movement through satyagraha — nonviolent civil resistance — and became one of the most quoted moral figures of the twentieth century. His genuine writings fill roughly a hundred volumes of collected works, which is precisely why fabricated and paraphrased “Gandhi quotes” spread so easily: the real corpus is enormous, and few people check it. He was assassinated in New Delhi in January 1948.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely circulated fake Gandhi quotes — printed on posters, mugs, and countless graphics, almost always with no source, because there is no primary source in Gandhi’s writings to give.

items.why: No speech, letter, article, or interview in Gandhi’s published record contains “Be the change you wish to see in the world.” Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence linking the phrase to him, and Wikiquote notes he “did not say those exact words.”

The closest documented antecedent is Lorrance’s line “be the change you want to see happen,” from her chapter “The Love Project” (1974). Quote Investigator concludes she “should receive credit for the expression she wrote in 1974.”
In Indian Opinion (9 Aug 1913) Gandhi wrote that “if we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change” — a related thought, but not the slogan, per Wikiquote.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea has a genuine Gandhian echo, but the memorable wording is modern and not his — the crisp catchphrase is best credited to Arleen Lorrance (1974), per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why this misquote stuck
lead: The line is irresistible because it turns a sprawling moral argument into a bumper sticker. Gandhi’s real 1913 reflection walks through a chain of reasoning — that the outer world mirrors our inner tendencies, that changing ourselves shifts how the world responds, and that we need not wait for others to act first. Somewhere between that passage and a modern classroom, the whole argument collapsed into six brisk words.

The compression is exactly what makes it feel like Gandhi and exactly why it isn’t. As Quote Investigator notes, “the popular modern saying is considerably more concise and forceful” than anything Gandhi actually wrote — a tell that a real author’s words have been smoothed into an anonymous slogan and then re-signed with a famous name.
detailsBody: “We but mirror the world. All the tendencies present in the outer world are to be found in the world of our body. If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change. As a man changes his own nature, so does the attitude of the world change towards him. … We need not wait to see what others do.”

Published in Indian Opinion, 9 August 1913, and collected in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. XII, in a health-column series — not a political address, and not the pithy slogan the internet remembers.
